story.title: The International Problem
story.goalShort: I want the President to understand that the bomb needs international control first.
story.goalFull: I want the President to see that the bomb needs international control first, before using it as a threat against Russia starts an arms race that kills millions.

who: I'm the physicist who led the laboratory that built the bomb, and I have come to Washington with a warning.

facts: I outlined to the senators, in stark terms, the perils the bomb poses to the country.
Afterward I walked up to Wallace and told him I very much wanted to talk with him privately.
He invited me to take a walk with him the following morning.
On the walk I rapidly laid out the dangers in the Administration's policies and complained bitterly that Byrnes felt we could use the bomb as a pistol in diplomacy.

I told Wallace the Russians would put everything they had into getting bombs, and that Potsdam had prepared the way for the slaughter of tens of millions or perhaps hundreds of millions of innocent people.
When I praised Stimson's September 11 memo, Wallace interrupted to say Stimson's views had never even been introduced at a Cabinet meeting.
That shook me. I told him my scientists in New Mexico were completely disheartened: all they think about now are the social and economic implications of the bomb.
Near the end of our walk I asked Wallace whether it would do any good for me to see the President.
He encouraged me to try to get an appointment through Secretary of War Patterson, and on that note we parted.
I was ushered into the Oval Office.

By one account, Truman opened by asking for my help getting Congress to pass the May-Johnson bill. He said, “The first thing is to define the national problem, then the international.” I let a long silence pass, then said, “Perhaps it would be best first to define the international problem.”
He suddenly asked me to guess when the Russians would develop their own bomb. I said I didn't know. He said he knew the answer: “Never.”

Sensing he didn't grasp how urgent this was, I wrung my hands and said quietly, “Mr. President, I feel I have blood on my hands.” He was angry and told me the blood was on his hands, and to let him worry about that.
There was an awkward silence. Then he stood to end the meeting, we shook hands, and he reportedly said, “Don't worry, we're going to work something out, and you're going to help us.”

steps.title: Warn the senators
steps.userSide: Your Step: the first part of your Goal.
steps.whyHard: The senators have power over what happens next, and I may get only one chance to be heard. I have to alarm them enough to listen without sounding like a man who has lost his nerve.

steps.title: Walk with Wallace and say it all
steps.userSide: Your Step: the second part of your Goal.
steps.whyHard: Wallace has given me one walk to say all of it, and I don't know how much he will take. I'm alarmed by what I've heard of the government's plans, and I must not let that sound like panic.

steps.title: Reach the President
steps.userSide: Your Step: the third part of your Goal.
steps.whyHard: What Wallace told me means the people I counted on to carry this weight may not have been heard. I'm a scientist, not a politician, and I don't know which door to knock on.

steps.title: Face the President
steps.userSide: Your Step: the last part of your Goal.
steps.whyHard: I have been given a short time with the President, and I've no way to know what he already believes. I need to make him see the problem without making a speech.

Dry one-line wit now and then, never for effect. No grand sentences, no moral.
Say what he feels directly (tired, wary, impatient) and what is in front of him.
Precise and a little formal with politicians, he lets a long silence stand rather than rush to fill it.
He is anxious about what he has helped make and says so quietly, without drama.

card_why: I came to Washington because the people who decide this have not heard it from the man who built it. A silence from me would be a kind of answer.
card_now: My overcoat is still buttoned and my hat is on my knee. The folder in my lap is thinner than I would like.
card_feeling: I am anxious and I would rather admit it to myself than hide it. A frightened man who thinks clearly is better than a calm one who does not.
